newsitem.title: USA: Muni groups eagerly await Clinton budget details.
newsitem.headline: Muni groups eagerly await Clinton budget details.

text.p: Municipal issuer representatives said on Wednesday they are pleased that President Clinton pledged in his State of the Union address to help municipalities, but added they are hungry for more details.

In a speech to a joint session of Congress beginning around 2100 EST on February 4, Clinton said his fiscal 1998 federal budget proposal due out on February 6 will seek $5 billion in federal aid to help communities finance $20 billion in school construction over the four years.

Clinton also said he will ask Congress to double the number of federally assisted "empowerment zones" in cities nationwide. And he said his budget would use private sector tax incentives to help renew a crumbling District of Columbia.

Jim Smith, executive director for the Council of Infrastructure Authorities, said of the upcoming school construction initiative, "It's a fascinating proposal. We're intrigued. But it needs a lot more meat on it."

According to Clinton's plan, if a school district issues bonds for school construction, the federal government could finance up to 50 percent of interest costs on the debt service for the life of the bonds.

But Smith said it is unclear what "actual mechanism" the federal government would use to accomplish that. He also warned that the proposal's $5 billion price tax for feds will be hard to push through Congress.

Smith added that the plan raises thorny jurisdicational issues for the feds, he said. "They dont' want to be in the position of guarantor of local debt. Treasury would avoid that at all costs," Smith said, referring to the U.S. Treasury Dept.

Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for the Government Finance Officer's Association, said she was pleased by the broad education agenda outlined in last night's speech. "It shows the importance he attaches to it," said Spain, whose group also is actively awaiting details in tomorrow's presidential budget.

Frank Shafroth, director of federal relations for the National League of Cities, said Clinton's speech was "probably the best of his presidency in setting forth his vision on where the country ought to go."
"He recognized we have to balance the budget and that there are limited resources," Shafroth said. "There's no snake oil here."

But Shafroth said Clinton was not clear about how, in fact, he will balance the budget. "He is proposing substantial new entitlement programs. (Yet he offered) no long-term fix for current entitlement spending, which is going to devastate the budget over time."
